label: Franks Violation — False Statement or Material Omission in Affidavit
motion_heading: The Defendant Is Entitled to a Franks Hearing Because the Warrant Affidavit Contained Material Falsehoods or Omissions

trigger.description: Ask when a search was conducted pursuant to a warrant and there is reason to believe the supporting affidavit contained inaccuracies or omissions.

excluded_explanations.display_note: The available evidence suggests simple negligence or mistake by the affiant, which does not meet the Franks standard (requires deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard for the truth). If discovery reveals greater culpability, this issue may become viable.

rule_statements.text: A defendant is entitled to an evidentiary hearing on the validity of a search warrant affidavit upon a substantial preliminary showing that the affiant knowingly and intentionally, or with reckless disregard for the truth, included a false statement in the affidavit that was necessary to the finding of probable cause.
The same analysis applies to material omissions from the affidavit, not just affirmative false statements.

If, after excising the false material or including the omitted information, the affidavit's remaining content is insufficient to establish probable cause, the warrant must be voided and the fruits of the search excluded.

practice_notes: A Franks hearing requires more than pointing to an error — the defense must make a substantial preliminary showing of deliberate falsehood or reckless disregard, not mere negligence.
Request the officer's underlying notes, dispatch recordings, or informant file in discovery before filing — they're often the source of the contradiction.
Consider pairing this with a good-faith exception rebuttal (Leon), since a Franks violation is one of the recognized exceptions to good-faith reliance on a warrant.
_author_notes: omissions_extension has no authority yet, so it never renders. Franks itself addresses false statements; the omissions extension is circuit-level doctrine. A possible 9th Circuit source is United States v. Stanert, 762 F.2d 775 (9th Cir. 1985) — unverified. Alaska authority not yet researched.
